assessmentSummary.identity: An upright sprint through athlete-spaced mini-hurdle wickets that constrain step rhythm and contact location during a max-velocity-oriented run.
currentCardFindings: The card names front-side cycle, elastic contact, and upright posture but does not define wicket height, number, individualized spacing, run-in, run-out, or progression rules.
Controlled equipment, environment, anatomy, load, fatigue, and complete difficulty fields are empty.
Uniform 40 difficulty values substantially understate spacing judgment, coordination, equipment setup, supervision, and error consequences.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain a wicket-run definition because the environmental constraint and equipment materially change execution and coaching. Require individualized spacing, a progressive run-in, clear run-out, low wicket height, and immediate regression when the athlete reaches, chops, clips wickets, or loses rhythm.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Wicket Run Max Velocity is a max velocity & rhythm exercise for speed, sprinting, and quick-release athletes. It emphasizes front side cycle, elastic foot contact, upright posture while keeping the session intent aligned with the Vortex phase sequence.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Training and Development of Elite Sprint Performance: an Integration of Scientific and Best Practice Literature
claims: Flying sprints use a progressive run-in to reach high velocity before a short maximal-velocity zone.
Wicket Run Max Velocity must separate run-in distance, measured fly-zone distance, intent, and timing method from its stable exercise identity.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Training and Development of Elite Sprint Performance: an Integration of Scientific and Best Practice Literature
claims: Acceleration, maximal velocity, and speed endurance are related but distinct sprint-training qualities.
Wicket Run Max Velocity belongs to upright high-speed locomotion; dense repeated-sprint conditioning requires a separate delivery profile.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Influence of Weekly Sprint Volume and Maximal Velocity Exposures on Eccentric Hamstring Strength in Professional Football Players
claims: Maximal-velocity exposures impose meaningful eccentric hamstring demand in addition to whole-lower-limb and trunk demands.
The card should identify bilateral hip, knee, and ankle actions, posterior-chain loading, calf-foot stiffness demand, and trunk-pelvis control.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Need for Speed—Improving Sprinting Performance in Football Players
claims: Mini-hurdle wickets provide external spacing cues intended to support upright posture, front-side action, and powerful knee lift.
Spacing should respond to athlete speed and stature; wickets must not be used to force reaching or an artificial universal stride length.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Longitudinal Effects of Resisted and Assisted Sprint Training on Sprint Kinematics, Acceleration, and Maximum Velocity: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
claims: Unresisted flying, resisted, assisted, and combined sprint methods create materially different kinematic and force-velocity demands.
Exercise difficulty must score physical demand and technical complexity directly, including coordination, supervision, impact, and failure consequence; it must not use a skill-library level.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Influence of Weekly Sprint Volume and Maximal Velocity Exposures on Eccentric Hamstring Strength in Professional Football Players
claims: Weekly high-speed sprint exposure can measurably affect eccentric hamstring force capacity.
Wicket Run Max Velocity needs explicit high-speed distance, contact, neural-intent, posterior-chain stress, performance-drop, session-recovery, and weekly-exposure tracking.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Need for Speed—Improving Sprinting Performance in Football Players
claims: Wicket runs require measured mini-hurdle placement on a safe track or turf surface.
The card needs wicket height, count, athlete-specific spacing, build-in, lane width, run-out, footwear, collision control, and coach placement.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Need for Speed—Improving Sprinting Performance in Football Players
claims: Wicket-run volume should be prescribed as quality repetitions with complete zone and equipment setup rather than as an unspecified drill count.
Progress spacing only when the athlete clears the wickets without reaching, chopping, clipping, or losing upright rhythm.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Need for Speed—Improving Sprinting Performance in Football Players
claims: The athlete should accelerate progressively into upright high-speed mechanics rather than attack the fly zone from a cold or abrupt start.
Use a small number of observable cues: build smoothly, run tall without leaning back, strike beneath the body, keep arm action coordinated, sprint through the zone, and decelerate gradually.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Influence of Weekly Sprint Volume and Maximal Velocity Exposures on Eccentric Hamstring Strength in Professional Football Players
claims: High-speed sprint load and recent exposure must be monitored rather than inferred from repetition count alone.
Stop for pain, hamstring or calf tightness, limping, stumble, unsafe surface or spacing, repeated overstriding, loss of upright control, or a persistent velocity or timing decline.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Training and Development of Elite Sprint Performance: an Integration of Scientific and Best Practice Literature
claims: Flying sprints are used to develop maximal velocity and should continue only while velocity and mechanics remain stable.
Wicket Run Max Velocity belongs early in a session after preparation and before fatigue-oriented work; rehabilitation, conditioning, and assisted-speed uses require separate contextual profiles.
Fly-in work isolates a short maximal-velocity action zone after an acceleration zone.
Athlete-facing support should show the zone layout, define a successful rep, limit the cue count, state the run-out expectation, and explain the stop signal.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Need for Speed—Improving Sprinting Performance in Football Players
claims: Coaches can use marked fly zones and timing to observe or monitor top-speed performance.
Coach support should include setup measurements, athlete-specific build-in choice, contact and posture observations, split consistency, spacing control, regression choices, and recovery decisions.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: Speed work should be developmentally appropriate and follow movement competency, readiness, and progressive exposure.
Intent, run-in length, fly-zone length, timing pressure, cue complexity, wicket spacing, and total exposure can be scaled without assigning the exercise a skill level.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Longitudinal Effects of Resisted and Assisted Sprint Training on Sprint Kinematics, Acceleration, and Maximum Velocity: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
claims: Normal, resisted, assisted, and combined sprinting produce different training conditions and should not be collapsed into one undifferentiated card.
Fly-zone length is dosage, run-in style is usually a variant, and external assistance or resistance may require a distinct definition when it changes the primary stimulus and safety model.

alternateAssessments.name: Mini-Hurdle Wicket Run
alternateAssessments.rationale: This name makes the existing equipment constraint explicit without changing the exercise.

alternateAssessments.name: Wicket Run with Extended Spacing
alternateAssessments.rationale: Spacing is individualized setup metadata and should be progressed within the card rather than creating a new identity.

alternateAssessments.name: Wicket Run to Flying 10
alternateAssessments.rationale: Adding a timed or marked fly zone after the wickets changes the delivery structure while retaining wicket-constrained entry mechanics.

alternateAssessments.name: Dribble Wicket Run
alternateAssessments.rationale: A dribble action through close wickets changes limb-cycle amplitude and speed while retaining the external rhythm constraint.

alternateAssessments.name: Assisted Wicket Sprint
alternateAssessments.rationale: Combining wickets with external assistance materially changes speed, equipment, supervision, and failure consequence.
